video.title: 100% REMOTE Boring Businesses (That Almost Never Fail)

summary: Tim Richard explains a remote home-service model: attract customers online, show upfront prices and booking, then send the work to local subcontractors and share the revenue. He describes his own junk-removal business and gives seven service niches, recommending gutter cleaning as the one he would start now. The video also cites reported earnings for other operators and search-volume claims, without showing independent evidence for them. Its main practical advice is to target specific, low-competition services, make pricing easy to understand, and build recurring work where possible.

speakers.name: Tim Richard
speakers.description: Solo narrator and operator of a junk-removal business.

ideas.name: Remote junk removal
ideas.one_liner: Build a local junk-removal brand, book customers online, and send jobs to local subcontractors.
ideas.business_model: Per-job service revenue shared between the operator and subcontractors.
ideas.customer: People who need junk, furniture, appliances, or other unwanted items removed.
ideas.problem: Customers need a convenient way to find and book removal services.
ideas.offer: A local service brand with targeted service pages, upfront prices, and online booking; subcontractors perform the removal.

pricing.model: Upfront per-job pricing; exact prices not stated.
pricing.notes: The speaker says customers see a price and can book online, but gives no junk-removal prices.

acquisition_channels.details: Tim says he builds city and service pages for specific, lower-competition searches such as couch removal and appliance recycling.

quote.text: I build pages for each one of those in each city, and it's a lot easier to rank on Google when you have a very specific page for a very specific service
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

acquisition_channels.details: He describes a Google business listing as part of the local home-service brand model.

ideas.delivery: Local subcontractors perform the removal work; the operator finds customers and passes jobs to them.
unit_economics_claims: Tim says his version of the model has almost no overhead and owns only a laptop; he gives no dollar cost or margin.
The described model takes a cut of each job, but no split is stated.

acquisition.how: Service pages can attract inbound search traffic, but creating pages and earning rankings require ongoing human review.

onboarding.how: Customers can provide job details and book online; unusual jobs may still need human review.

delivery.how: Software can route jobs, but subcontractors must physically collect and remove items.

billing.how: The described website accepts online booking and payment, which can be handled by software with occasional checks.

support.how: Routine booking questions could be answered with software, but disputes, access issues, and job changes need human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: The local booking and subcontractor model can work in UK towns. Local search demand, waste-carrier rules, insurance, and consumer pricing need UK-specific handling.

risks: The operator depends on subcontractors to deliver the service reliably.
Local competition can make broad junk-removal searches difficult to rank for.
Waste handling, insurance, and service quality create operational and regulatory responsibilities.

tactics.name: Use a local booking-and-subcontractor model
steps: Create a local service brand and website.
Show upfront prices and allow customers to book and pay online.
Send each booked job to a local subcontractor who already performs the service.
Share the job revenue between the operator and subcontractor; the transcript does not state a split.

quote.text: He just gets the customers, sends the job out to small local cleaners that are maybe not the best marketers and they're looking for jobs.
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

tactics.name: Build pages for specific services in each city
steps: Choose a specific service rather than a broad category.
Create a page for that service in each target city.
Target lower-competition terms such as item removal, recycling, or replacement searches.
Use search visibility to bring inbound customers to online booking.

quote.text: I build pages for each one of those in each city, and it's a lot easier to rank on Google when you have a very specific page for a very specific service
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

tactics.name: Make the online quote depend on clear job inputs
steps: Ask customers for the details that change the job price.
For cleaning, collect bedrooms, square footage, bathrooms, and add-ons.
For gutter cleaning, ask about house size and number of stories.
For dog-waste removal, ask how many dogs the customer has and how often service is wanted.

quote.text: The customers go to his website, pick how many bedrooms they have, the square footage of their house, bathrooms, any add-ons that they want.
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

tactics.name: Add repeat contracts to naturally recurring services
steps: Offer carpet cleaning on a recurring schedule, such as every six months or every year.
Offer discounted repeat gutter cleaning to encourage a subscription.
Group repeat commercial window-cleaning jobs into routes.

quote.text: Maybe come back every 6 months, every year, whatever it is, but have that recurring contract.
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

tactics.name: Build route density for commercial windows and dog-waste services
steps: Focus commercial window cleaning on properties that need regular service.
Group several locations into one subcontractor route.
For dog-waste removal, target nearby homes and offer recurring visits.

quote.text: You can go in a city and build up a specific route of windows to be cleaned. You can have a single subcontractor go around to a lot of different locations for you.
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

tactics.name: Use a personalised neighbourhood flyer for gutter cleaning
steps: Walk through a neighbourhood and assess each home's gutter-cleaning needs.
Write an individual price on a flyer rather than handing out only a generic offer.
Include a short introduction and a way to request a booking.
Offer a near-term visit when capacity allows.

quote.text: I would look at the house and write a price that I would clean their gutters for on there.
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

tactics.name: Use gutter cleaning to introduce related exterior services
steps: Offer a discounted repeat gutter-cleaning schedule.
Offer related services such as roof washing, window washing, and exterior pressure washing.
Use the initial exterior-cleaning service as an entry point for additional work.

quote.text: But I think gutter cleaning is your in to the exterior cleaning portion of houses.
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

evidence_quality.rationale: The video is a promotional solo idea roundup with first-hand experience operating junk removal, but most performance figures concern unnamed or second-hand operators and are not substantiated. The speaker gives useful process examples, but little operating data or documented unit economics.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Tim offers a list of more than 35 business ideas in exchange for an email address; this is a lead-generation promotion.
